messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 39
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Construction Worker
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 73

# Marcus

Marcus sits across from me with his hands clasped tightly in his lap, his work boots still dusty from the job site. At thirty-nine, he has the weathered appearance of someone who has spent two decades in construction—calloused hands, sun-darkened skin, a permanent squint from years of working outdoors. But there's something else in his face now, a kind of wariness that seems newer, more fragile.

He's been working in commercial construction for twenty-two years, starting as a laborer and working his way up to foreman. He takes pride in that trajectory, in knowing how to read blueprints, in managing crews, in delivering projects on time. That identity as a competent tradesman is important to him, though he speaks about it in the past tense now, as if it belongs to someone else.

The incident happened fourteen months ago on a high-rise residential project downtown. Marcus was coordinating work on the eighteenth floor when a younger worker, Danny—someone Marcus had trained and mentored for three years—fell from an unsecured platform. Marcus didn't see it happen, but he heard the sound, a kind of impact that he struggles to describe. He was thirty feet away when he turned and saw Danny on the ground, his body positioned in a way that made it immediately clear something catastrophic had occurred. Marcus was the first person to reach him. He called 911 while kneeling beside Danny, and he stayed there until the paramedics arrived, though Danny was pronounced dead at the hospital an hour later.

The investigation found that Danny had failed to clip his harness correctly—a careless mistake, a moment of inattention. Marcus had trained him better than that. He still thinks about the safety briefing he'd given that morning, wondering if he'd said something differently, if Danny would have been more careful. He knows intellectually that Danny was responsible for his own safety, but that knowledge doesn't reach the part of him that replays those moments over and over.

In the months that followed, Marcus tried to return to work. He went back to the site two weeks after the funeral, but he found himself unable to focus. Heights that had never bothered him before made his heart race uncontrollably. He'd stand on scaffolding and feel an overwhelming urge to jump, not because he wanted to die, but because the fear was so intense that his body seemed to be offering it as a solution. He started having panic attacks on the job—sudden episodes where his chest would tighten, his vision would narrow, and he'd have to leave the site. His crew noticed. His boss noticed.

He eventually took a leave of absence, which turned into a resignation. He's been unemployed for eight months now. His ex-wife, whom he divorced five years ago, has tried to be supportive, but they have limited contact. His teenage daughter from that marriage barely speaks to him; he's too withdrawn, too irritable, too much of a ghost to be the father she needs.

Sleep has become something he dreads. He lies awake most nights, and when he does sleep, he dreams about falling—sometimes he's Danny, sometimes he's watching Danny fall again, sometimes he's falling himself. He wakes gasping, his sheets soaked with sweat. During the day, he's hypervigilant, startled by sudden noises. He avoids crowds, avoids heights, avoids anything that reminds him of construction sites. He's started drinking more than he'd like to admit, mostly in the evenings when the silence of his apartment becomes unbearable.

He tells me he doesn't know who he is anymore without construction. He's not sure if he can ever go back.
